FINAL PAYCHECK DELIVERY METHOD AND LOCATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

FINAL WAGE DELIVERY METHOD AND LOCATION
Re: Final Paycheck Delivery — Jordan Lee

This document concerns the employment of Jordan Lee, whose employment with Acme, Inc. ended on October 1, 2026. The separation is described here as: discharge.

California Labor Code section 208 sets a place-of-payment rule for final wages that depends on how the employment ended, and separate provisions of the same article address mailed payment and direct deposit as payment methods. For this separation, final wages were, or are to be, delivered as follows:

Delivery method: mailed to designated address

Delivery address or location: 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103

If payment was made or requested by mail, the date of mailing is noted here as: October 1, 2026.

WHERE FINAL WAGES MUST BE DELIVERED: THE STATUTORY PLACE-OF-PAYMENT RULE
Separately from when final wages are due, California law also addresses where a discharged or quitting employee's final wages must be delivered. The statute distinguishes the two situations: an employee who is discharged must be paid at the place of discharge, while an employee who quits must be paid at the office or agency of the employer in the county where the employee has been performing labor. This letter treats October 1, 2026 as the date Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. ended, based on a separation described here as: discharge.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every employee who is discharged shall be paid at the place of discharge, and every employee who quits shall be paid at the office or agency of the employer in the county where the employee has been performing labor. All payments shall be made in the manner provided by law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 208, Cal. Lab. Code § 208 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=208.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the place-of-payment rule for a discharged versus a quitting employee — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular separation, and not a claim about where this particular final paycheck was, or should have been, delivered. The statute also states that '[a]ll payments shall be made in the manner provided by law,' a cross-reference to the article's other payment-method provisions (including the mailing and direct-deposit rules addressed in separate clauses) rather than an independent, self-contained rule in its own right. This is a single statutory section (§ 208); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

THE MAILING OPTION FOR FINAL WAGES AND ITS EFFECT ON THE PAYMENT DATE
California law gives some, but not all, separating employees a statutory right to have final wages mailed rather than delivered in person. An employee who quits without giving the employer at least 72 hours' notice is entitled to receive payment by mail if the employee requests it and designates a mailing address, and the date of mailing is treated as the date of payment for purposes of the 72-hour payment deadline that applies to that kind of quit. A comparable statutory right to demand mailed payment exists for a discharged employee only in one narrow category: an employer laying off a group of employees due to the end of seasonal employment in curing, canning, or drying perishable fruit, fish, or vegetables must make payment by mail to any employee in that group who requests it and designates a mailing address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Notwithstanding any other law, an employee who quits without providing a 72-hour notice shall be entitled to receive payment by mail if he or she so requests and designates a mailing address. The date of the mailing shall constitute the date of payment for purposes of the requirement to provide payment within 72 hours of the notice of quitting."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 202(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 202, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=202.)
  "provided, however, that the reasonable time shall not exceed 72 hours, and further provided that payment shall be made by mail to any employee who so requests and designates a mailing address therefor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 201(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 201, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when a mailed-payment option is expressly available and how the mailing date interacts with a payment deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular separation, and not a claim that a mailed-payment right exists for every kind of discharge or quit. Outside the two situations quoted below (a no-notice quit, and a seasonal perishable-food-industry group layoff), this research did not locate express statutory text giving a general right to demand mailed final-wage payment for an ordinary discharge or for a quit preceded by 72 hours' notice; that gap is disclosed here rather than assumed away, since silence in a statute is not the same as a prohibition and is not treated as one by this clause. The two citations below come from two separate statutory sections (§§ 201(a) and 202(a)) and are independent sources of each other.

DIRECT DEPOSIT AND FINAL WAGES
California's general wage-payment-method statute permits an employer to pay wages by direct deposit into an account of the employee's choice, with the employee's voluntary authorization, and separately addresses using direct deposit for a final paycheck: where an employee is discharged or quits, the employer may pay the wages earned and unpaid at that time by direct deposit, provided the employer complies with the same statutory provisions that otherwise govern payment of wages upon termination or quitting. The statute does not, in its own text, spell out additional mechanics — such as a shortened bank-processing window or a requirement that deposited funds be immediately available to the employee — beyond that cross-reference back to the termination and quitting payment rules.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If an employer discharges an employee or the employee quits, the employer may pay the wages earned and unpaid at the time the employee is discharged or quits by making a deposit authorized pursuant to this subdivision, provided that the employer complies with the provisions of this article relating to the payment of wages upon termination or quitting of employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 213(d), Cal. Lab. Code § 213, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=213.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's direct-deposit statute actually says about final wages — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payment, and not a claim that California imposes a special, self-contained direct-deposit rule of the kind some other states have adopted for final paychecks (for example, requiring funds to be available on the regular payday regardless of the bank's normal processing time). No such additional, freestanding rule was located in this section or elsewhere in this research session; that absence is disclosed here rather than papered over with a citation that does not actually say it. What the statute does establish is narrower and procedural: direct deposit of final wages is conditioned on the employer otherwise complying with the applicable termination-or-quitting payment provisions, which is what determines the deadline by which those wages are due regardless of the payment method chosen. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 213(d)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

THE ITEMIZED WAGE STATEMENT REQUIREMENT STILL APPLIES TO A FINAL PAYCHECK
California's itemized-wage-statement requirement is not excused because a particular paycheck happens to be an employee's last one: the statute requires an employer to furnish an itemized statement semimonthly or at the time of each payment of wages, without carving out a final payment. This document set already contains a dedicated, separately verified clause covering that requirement in full — including its specific nine-item list, its penalty structure, and its own disclosed limits — and does not re-derive that content here; this clause exists only to confirm that a final paycheck does not fall outside it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer, semimonthly or at the time of each payment of wages, shall furnish to their employee, either as a detachable part of the check, draft, or voucher paying the employee’s wages, or separately if wages are paid by personal check or cash, an accurate itemized statement in writing showing"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that the itemized-wage-statement requirement applies to a final wage payment on the same terms as any other — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payment, and not a claim about the statement's full content, which the corpus's dedicated wage-statement clauses address separately rather than duplicating here. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 226(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYER FINAL-WAGE TIMING — APPLICABILITY NOTE
California Labor Code section 201.3 sets final-wage timing rules that apply specifically to an employee of a "temporary services employer" (a staffing agency) — a different, more specific set of deadlines from the general final-paycheck timing rules in Labor Code sections 201 and 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns Jordan Lee's assignment, through Acme, Inc., to perform work for Client Corp, an assignment recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. Section 201.3's specialized schedules turn on the statute's own functional definition of "temporary services employer" and on how a given assignment or the underlying employment relationship ended, both described in the information that follows. Naming Acme, Inc. and Client Corp here does not itself determine that Acme, Inc. meets the statutory definition of a "temporary services employer," and does not determine which of the statute's several payment schedules applies to this particular assignment.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYER" FOR THIS SECTION
Labor Code section 201.3 defines "temporary services employer," for purposes of that section's own timing rules, as an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers and that performs a specific set of functions with respect to those workers: negotiating with clients over matters such as timing, work type, working conditions, and price; determining worker assignments or reassignments (even if a worker may refuse a specific assignment); retaining authority to reassign a worker a client finds unacceptable; assigning or reassigning workers; setting workers' rate of pay; paying workers from its own account; and retaining the right to hire and terminate workers. The statute excludes three categories from that definition even if they otherwise supply workers to clients: a bona fide nonprofit organization, a farm labor contractor as separately defined in the Labor Code, and a garment manufacturing employer as separately defined in the Labor Code. The statute also defines "client" and "customer," for this section's purposes, as the person with whom the temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more of its employees, and it borrows the Unemployment Insurance Code's definition of "employing unit" as a component of its own definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Temporary services employer” means an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers to perform services for the clients or customers and that performs all of the following functions:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "“Temporary services employer” does not include any of the following: (A) A bona fide nonprofit organization that provides temporary service employees to clients. (B) A farm labor contractor, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1682. (C) A garment manufacturing employer, which, for purposes of this section, has the same meaning as “contractor,” as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 2671."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer exclusions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "“Client” and “customer” mean the person with whom a temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more individuals employed by the temporary services employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, client/customer definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivision (a)), used as real evidence of how this specific section defines "temporary services employer" for purposes of the final-wage timing rules addressed in the other clauses here — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not itself a determination that any particular staffing arrangement meets or fails this definition. The seven functional criteria in paragraph (a)(1), subparts (A) through (G), are paraphrased in the body above rather than quoted in full; only that paragraph's introductory sentence is quoted below as an exact, contiguous excerpt, along with the full text of the exclusions in paragraph (a)(2) and the "client"/"customer" definition in paragraph (a)(4). This definition cross-references other statutes this clause did not independently fetch or verify: the definition of "employing unit" in Unemployment Insurance Code section 135, the farm-labor-contractor definition in Labor Code section 1682(b), and the garment-manufacturing "contractor" definition in Labor Code section 2671(d) — an honest gap, disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. All three citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.3(a); they are treated as one source describing related definitional provisions, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

THE GENERAL RULE: WEEKLY PAYMENT TIED TO PAYROLL WEEKS, NOT TO WHEN THE ASSIGNMENT ENDS
Subject to several exceptions stated elsewhere in the same section, Labor Code section 201.3 provides that when an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client, that employee's wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly — regardless of when the specific assignment ends — with wages for a given calendar week due by the regular payday of the following calendar week. The statute states that a temporary services employer who pays on that weekly schedule is deemed to have timely paid the employee's wages upon completion of the assignment, meaning the assignment's end date, standing alone, does not accelerate the payment deadline the way the general discharge and quit rules can. A parallel, narrower provision applies to a security guard employed by a temporary services employer in the security services industry who is registered under a specified Business and Professions Code licensing chapter and employed by a licensed private patrol operator: for that category of worker, the statute uses a "workweek" as defined elsewhere in the Labor Code, rather than a calendar week, as the measuring period, with wages due by the regular payday of the following workweek. The same section states that a temporary services employer who violates this section is subject to the civil penalties provided in Labor Code section 203, and to any other penalties available at law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in paragraphs (2) to (5), inclusive, if an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client, that employee’s wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly, regardless of when the assignment ends, and wages for work performed during any calendar week shall be due and payable not later than the regular payday of the following calendar week. A temporary services employer shall be deemed to have timely paid wages upon completion of an assignment if wages are paid in compliance with this subdivision."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, general weekly final-wage timing rule for temporary services employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "Except as provided in paragraphs (2) to (5), inclusive, if an employee of a temporary services employer in the security services industry is a security guard who is registered pursuant to Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 7580) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, is employed by a private patrol operator licensed pursuant to that chapter, and is assigned to work for a client, that employee’s wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly, regardless of when the assignment ends, and wages for work performed during any workweek, as defined under Section 500, shall be due and payable not later than the regular payday of the following workweek."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, security-guard sub-rule using a workweek measuring period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "A temporary services employer who violates this section is subject to the civil penalties provided for in Section 203 and to any other penalties available at law."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, civil penalty for a violation of this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(1)(A), (b)(1)(B), and (c)), used as real evidence of the default weekly-payment schedule this section sets for temporary services employees and of the penalty the section itself invokes for a violation — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that this default schedule applies without exception. The statute expressly makes this rule subject to paragraphs (2) through (5) of the same subdivision (the day-to-day, trade-dispute, discharge, and quit provisions addressed in this corpus's other Section 201.3 clauses) and, separately, to the 90-consecutive-day provision in paragraph (6); none of those exceptions are restated here. This clause does not independently verify that the security-guard sub-rule's licensing prerequisites — registration under Business and Professions Code Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 7580) and employment by a private patrol operator licensed under that chapter — are met in any particular case. Nor does this clause restate what a "regular payday" is for a given employer, or the substantive mechanics of the Section 203 waiting-time penalty (its accrual rate and 30-day cap), which this corpus addresses in a separate, dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document rather than duplicating here. The three citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.3; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

TWO EXCEPTIONS REQUIRING DAILY PAYMENT INSTEAD OF WEEKLY
Labor Code section 201.3 sets two situations in which a temporary services employee's wages are due and payable at the end of each day, rather than on the section's general weekly schedule, regardless of when the assignment itself ends. The first applies to an employee assigned to work for a client on a day-to-day basis, but only if three conditions are all met: the employee reports to or assembles at the temporary services employer's office (or another specified location); the employee is dispatched to a client's worksite each day and returns to or reports to that office or location upon completing the day's assignment; and the employee's work does not fall within the executive, administrative, or professional classifications defined in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and is not clerical work. The second applies without those three conditions: an employee assigned to work for a client that is engaged in a trade dispute is paid daily.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client on a day-to-day basis, that employee’s wages are due and payable at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends, if each of the following occurs: (A) The employee reports to or assembles at the office of the temporary services employer or other location. (B) The employee is dispatched to a client’s worksite each day and returns to or reports to the office of the temporary services employer or other location upon completion of the assignment. (C) The employee’s work is not executive, administrative, or professional, as defined in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and is not clerical."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, daily payment for a day-to-day assignment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client engaged in a trade dispute, that employee’s wages are due and payable at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, daily payment for a client engaged in a trade dispute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(2) and (b)(3)), used as real evidence that these two situations trigger daily rather than weekly payment — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular assignment is or is not a day-to-day assignment or a trade-dispute assignment within the meaning of this statute. The day-to-day exception's three conditions are quoted in full below as one contiguous excerpt from paragraph (b)(2); whether a given assignment in fact satisfies all three — particularly whether specific job duties are "executive, administrative, or professional" or "clerical" — depends on the separate body of Industrial Welfare Commission wage-order classification law, which this clause does not reproduce or apply here. The statute does not itself define "trade dispute" within Section 201.3; this clause does not supply that definition from elsewhere. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.3(b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

WHEN THE TEMP EMPLOYEE'S OWN EMPLOYMENT ENDS: REVERSION TO THE GENERAL DISCHARGE AND QUIT RULES
Labor Code section 201.3 distinguishes between an assignment ending (addressed by the section's own weekly or daily schedules described elsewhere in this material) and the temporary services employee's employment with the temporary services employer itself ending. Where an employee assigned to work for a client is discharged by the temporary services employer (the statute's text also refers to a "leasing employer" in this same provision, without separately defining that term), the statute directs that wages are due and payable as provided in Labor Code section 201 — the general immediate-payment-on-discharge rule — rather than under Section 201.3's own weekly or daily schedules. Where such an employee instead quits their employment with the temporary services employer, the statute directs that wages are due and payable as provided in Labor Code section 202 — the general quitting-employee rule, including its 72-hour and notice-based timing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client and is discharged by the temporary services employer or leasing employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Section 201."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, discharge reverts to Section 201 timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client and quits his or her employment with the temporary services employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Section 202."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, quitting reverts to Section 202 timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(4) and (b)(5)), used as real evidence that a discharge or a quit of the underlying employment relationship — as opposed to the mere ending of one client assignment — reverts the applicable timing rule to the general Section 201 or Section 202 standard, not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular separation was in fact a discharge, a quit, or merely the end of one assignment within a continuing employment relationship. This clause does not restate the substantive content of Section 201 or Section 202 themselves (their own payment deadlines and mailing options), which this corpus addresses in its dedicated Final Paycheck Delivery Method and Location document rather than duplicating here. The statutory text as fetched uses the phrase "leasing employer" in paragraph (b)(4) without defining it elsewhere within Section 201.3; that term is quoted as the statute states it, and this clause does not resolve what distinguishes a "leasing employer" from a "temporary services employer" for this purpose — an honest gap, disclosed rather than guessed at. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.3(b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

A 90-CONSECUTIVE-DAY ASSIGNMENT LIMIT, AND THIS SECTION'S OWN NON-LIMITATION CLAUSE
Labor Code section 201.3 places an outer time limit on its own weekly-payment default: if an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for the same client for more than 90 consecutive calendar days, the section stops applying to that assignment unless the temporary services employer is already paying the employee weekly in compliance with the section's own general rule. The same section also includes its own savings clause, stating that nothing in Section 201.3 is to be interpreted to limit any rights or remedies otherwise available to an employee under state or federal law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client for over 90 consecutive calendar days, this section does not apply unless the temporary services employer pays the employee weekly in compliance with paragraph (1) of subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(6) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, 90-consecutive-day limit on this section's applicability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "This section shall not be interpreted to limit any rights or remedies otherwise available under state or federal law."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, non-limitation of other rights or remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(6) and (d)), used as real evidence that a 90-consecutive-day assignment can take a temporary services employee outside this section's coverage, and that the section does not purport to cut off other legal rights or remedies — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular assignment has or has not reached 90 consecutive calendar days with a given client. The statute's own text, as fetched, does not state what timing rule governs a temporary services employee's wages once this section stops applying under paragraph (b)(6) and the employer was not already paying weekly; this clause does not resolve that gap by assuming which other Labor Code provision would then control. The statute also does not define "consecutive calendar days" for this purpose — for example, whether or how a gap in the assignment interrupts consecutiveness — and this clause does not supply that definition from elsewhere. The two citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.3; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF FINAL WAGE DELIVERY
Please sign below to acknowledge the delivery method and location recorded above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

Employer representative (on behalf of Acme, Inc.): _______________
Date: _______________

—

expectedJSON.body: California Labor Code section 201.3 sets final-wage timing rules that apply specifically to an employee of a "temporary services employer" (a staffing agency) — a different, more specific set of deadlines from the general final-paycheck timing rules in Labor Code sections 201 and 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns Jordan Lee's assignment, through Acme, Inc., to perform work for Client Corp, an assignment recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. Section 201.3's specialized schedules turn on the statute's own functional definition of "temporary services employer" and on how a given assignment or the underlying employment relationship ended, both described in the information that follows. Naming Acme, Inc. and Client Corp here does not itself determine that Acme, Inc. meets the statutory definition of a "temporary services employer," and does not determine which of the statute's several payment schedules applies to this particular assignment.

Labor Code section 201.3 defines "temporary services employer," for purposes of that section's own timing rules, as an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers and that performs a specific set of functions with respect to those workers: negotiating with clients over matters such as timing, work type, working conditions, and price; determining worker assignments or reassignments (even if a worker may refuse a specific assignment); retaining authority to reassign a worker a client finds unacceptable; assigning or reassigning workers; setting workers' rate of pay; paying workers from its own account; and retaining the right to hire and terminate workers. The statute excludes three categories from that definition even if they otherwise supply workers to clients: a bona fide nonprofit organization, a farm labor contractor as separately defined in the Labor Code, and a garment manufacturing employer as separately defined in the Labor Code. The statute also defines "client" and "customer," for this section's purposes, as the person with whom the temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more of its employees, and it borrows the Unemployment Insurance Code's definition of "employing unit" as a component of its own definition.

expectedJSON.body: Subject to several exceptions stated elsewhere in the same section, Labor Code section 201.3 provides that when an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client, that employee's wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly — regardless of when the specific assignment ends — with wages for a given calendar week due by the regular payday of the following calendar week. The statute states that a temporary services employer who pays on that weekly schedule is deemed to have timely paid the employee's wages upon completion of the assignment, meaning the assignment's end date, standing alone, does not accelerate the payment deadline the way the general discharge and quit rules can. A parallel, narrower provision applies to a security guard employed by a temporary services employer in the security services industry who is registered under a specified Business and Professions Code licensing chapter and employed by a licensed private patrol operator: for that category of worker, the statute uses a "workweek" as defined elsewhere in the Labor Code, rather than a calendar week, as the measuring period, with wages due by the regular payday of the following workweek. The same section states that a temporary services employer who violates this section is subject to the civil penalties provided in Labor Code section 203, and to any other penalties available at law.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code section 201.3 sets two situations in which a temporary services employee's wages are due and payable at the end of each day, rather than on the section's general weekly schedule, regardless of when the assignment itself ends. The first applies to an employee assigned to work for a client on a day-to-day basis, but only if three conditions are all met: the employee reports to or assembles at the temporary services employer's office (or another specified location); the employee is dispatched to a client's worksite each day and returns to or reports to that office or location upon completing the day's assignment; and the employee's work does not fall within the executive, administrative, or professional classifications defined in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and is not clerical work. The second applies without those three conditions: an employee assigned to work for a client that is engaged in a trade dispute is paid daily.
